title: Reading link previews before you click
body_md:
## A preview is a clue, not a permission slip

The label “View document” is text chosen by the sender. The link target is a separate address. Previewing it helps you notice a mismatch **before** navigation. It does not promise that the final destination or the content is safe. Some links redirect; a legitimate hosting service can contain a stranger's form; a mobile app may show only part of the address.

On a desktop, hovering may reveal the target in a status bar or tooltip. Read the entire visible host, not just a brand word on the left. On an iPhone in Safari, touching and holding a link opens a preview; other apps and phones behave differently. A preview may load page content, so for a truly untrusted link it can be better to leave the message and navigate independently. If an app hides or truncates the address, that is a reason to use another route, not to guess.

### Three things the preview can conceal

- **A shortener or tracking link** shows its intermediary domain. You cannot infer the eventual destination from its random code. Some legitimate newsletters use such links. For an important account action, open the service directly rather than submitting a sensitive URL to a third-party “unshortener.”
- **A redirect** can send you elsewhere after the first address. If you chose to browse independently and reach a sign-in or payment form, check the address bar at the moment you act. Do not enter data just because the first hop looked familiar.
- **Hosted content** lives on a real platform but may be authored by anyone with access. A real forms or document host confirms the host, not the person requesting credentials or payment. Verify the request with the supposed sender through another channel.

This is a triage tool. A clearly wrong domain is a stop signal. A plausible destination is still only one piece of evidence. A link in a message can be skipped entirely when a known app, bookmark or official contact route answers the underlying question.

### Try it safely

In a message you already trust, compare the button label to the displayed target without opening it. Notice whether your device shows the host, a shortener, or no usable address. The goal is to learn your interface, not to test a suspicious link by visiting it.

widget_config.goal: Use a link preview to identify uncertainty, then choose a separate route for sensitive actions.
widget_config.today_action: On a message you already trust, inspect one link without opening it and note whether your device reveals the full host.
widget_config.scope: General link-reading habit; interface examples are Safari on iPhone and desktop Gmail. Other apps vary. All exercise addresses are synthetic.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: a shortened payroll notice
blocks.situation: An email says a payslip is ready. The button preview shows https://go-payroll.example/r/7Q4 rather than the payroll service you normally use.
blocks.analysis: The short link hides what follows. It could be a legitimate notification service, but the email cannot establish that. Open your normal payroll portal or ask payroll through the known internal directory; do not submit the link to a public expansion tool.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: an ordinary tracking redirect
blocks.situation: A newsletter you requested links through https://mail-news.example/c/42 to an article on its own site. The label and tracking host differ.
blocks.analysis: Marketing redirects are common and this mismatch alone is not fraud. If the article is worth reading, visit the publisher from a saved bookmark or its independently found homepage. Never reuse the newsletter route for an unexpected account or payment request.

blocks.title: The scholarship form
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise. A student receives a message about a scholarship application; no real form is opened.

steps.prompt: The text says “Application status.” The preview shows a short link. What can you conclude?

choices.text: The university owns the final page because the message says so.
choices.consequence: You accept a claim the preview does not establish.
choices.explanation: A label and a short code do not reveal the owner of the final page.

choices.text: The final destination is unknown; use the university portal separately.
choices.consequence: You keep the link out of the decision.
choices.explanation: An independent portal can confirm the application status.

steps.prompt: You later check the portal; it has no alert. The message claims you must pay a processing charge. Next?

choices.text: Pay through the message before the deadline.
choices.consequence: You may send money based only on the unverified demand.
choices.explanation: A new financial demand needs independent confirmation.

choices.text: Contact the admissions office using the directory on the university site.
choices.consequence: The office can confirm the procedure.
choices.explanation: Use contact details found outside the message.

steps.prompt: Later, the office confirms a legitimate application form on a hosted platform. What does the host prove?

choices.text: The platform alone proves every field and payment instruction is authorized.
choices.consequence: You rely on hosting instead of the confirmed procedure.
choices.explanation: Hosted pages can be created by different people.

choices.text: Only where the page is hosted; compare its exact instructions with the office's guidance.
choices.consequence: You separate platform identity from form authorship.
choices.explanation: A real host is not a substitute for verifying the request.

steps.prompt: The form redirects to another site before a sign-in. Your move?

choices.text: Enter credentials because the first page was confirmed.
choices.consequence: The final sign-in destination remains unchecked.
choices.explanation: A redirect changes the page that receives your details.

choices.text: Stop and check the final address and expected sign-in method with the office.
choices.consequence: You verify the action at the moment it matters.
choices.explanation: A confirmed first hop does not authenticate later pages.

blocks.debrief: The preview showed uncertainty; the independent portal and office resolved it. Retry the choices that treated an intermediary or host as proof of the final request.

questions.prompt: A button says “Bank statement,” but the preview is a short URL. What is known?

choices.text: Only the first link's shortener host is visible; use your bank app for the statement.
choices.explanation: The code does not tell you the final destination.

choices.text: The bank is the final host because the label names it.

questions.prompt: A link opens a real document-hosting service and asks for a password. What does the host prove?

choices.text: That the document was authorized by the claimed sender.
choices.explanation: Hosting services can contain user-created material.

choices.text: Only the host; verify the request with the sender independently.
choices.explanation: The author and request still need checking.

questions.prompt: On your phone, a preview truncates the host. What should you do for an account change?

choices.text: Tap to see the rest, then decide.
choices.explanation: Following an untrusted link is unnecessary when a known route exists.

choices.text: Open the service through your saved app or bookmark.
choices.explanation: You can reach the task without guessing the hidden address.

questions.prompt: A requested newsletter uses a tracking redirect. Is that automatically phishing?

choices.text: No. Redirects can be legitimate; sensitive actions still need separate verification.
choices.explanation: A mismatch is a clue, not a complete diagnosis.

choices.text: Yes. Every redirected link is fraudulent.
